s: Part four.
Exploring a large codebase.
By the end of this part, you'll know why you search before you read, what should stay in the window, and what makes delegating the exploration worth it.
Let's start with a picture.
Suppose you need to know which of four hundred supplier contracts mention one particular company.
You could read all four hundred.
Nobody does.
You search the index.
You get a list of contracts and clause numbers.
And then you read just those clauses, closely.
Reading everything cover to cover leaves you exhausted.
You're holding four hundred contracts' worth of detail.
And you're still unsure you caught them all.
Exploring a large codebase is the same move, under one extra pressure.
The reading is not free.
And it does not go away once done.
Everything the model reads stays in front of it for the rest of the session.
Competing with everything it reads afterwards.
In exam terms, exploration is a retrieval problem.
And the winning pattern is search, then read.
Step one.
A symbol search, such as the Grep tool in Claude Code, covers the whole codebase cheaply.
It returns file paths and line numbers.
That's a map.
Step two.
Read only the matched ranges, plus enough surrounding lines to establish scope.
Step three.
Follow one level of definitions and callers.
Step four.
Write down what you learned, before going further.
And the opposite?
Reading files in the hope of encountering the symbol.
That's a linear scan, with no upper bound on cost, and no guarantee of completeness.
The notes give three reasons why reading whole files is usually wrong.
One.
The density is terrible.
A two-thousand-line service file typically holds perhaps thirty lines relevant to your question.
The other one thousand nine hundred and seventy sit in the window for the rest of the session.
Two.
It crowds out later evidence.
And because it usually lands in the middle of a long context, it's also the material the model uses least reliably.
Three.
It hides the structure you actually need.
Knowing which twelve files reference a symbol tells you more about a change's blast radius than reading any one of them completely.
Question one.
Here's the scenario.
Before a refactor, a developer asks Claude Code to find every call site of a deprecated charge-card function, in a three-thousand-file monorepo.
The first attempt read the payments directory file by file, and used most of the window before the refactor started.
The developer needs two things.
A complete list.
And a main session with room left for implementation.
What's the right approach?
Take a second.
The answer.
Search for the symbol to get paths and line numbers.
Read only the matched ranges.
And delegate the wide sweep to a subagent that returns file-and-line hits.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: read the payments and billing directories in full first, because most call sites probably live there.
Why?
Terrible density.
And no completeness guarantee outside those directories.
Wrong: load the whole repository into the large window, so nothing is missed.
Why?
It maximises cost and minimises density.
And recall degrades as the window fills, even when it fits.
Wrong: list every file, and read each in turn with a running prose summary.
Why?
That's an unbounded scan.
And its summaries drop the exact paths and line numbers the refactor needs.
Notice that last one.
Prose summaries losing identifiers is the same failure we met in part one, in a different costume.
Takeaway.
Search to build a map, then read only what the map points to.
The second concept is what stays in the window.
The plain version.
You want to see who is affected by a changed office policy.
You don't photocopy every employee's full file.
You pull the list of people the policy applies to.
Then you read the one relevant line in each file.
The list alone tells you most of how far the change reaches.
The technical name is just-in-time retrieval, from Anthropic's context engineering guidance.
Keep lightweight identifiers in context.
Paths, symbol names, and line ranges.
And load content through tools only when it's needed.
Hold on to this line.
Identifiers, not content.
Question two.
Here's the scenario.
An engineer wants the blast radius of renaming a widely used config loader.
The current prompt pastes the diff, plus the full contents of all sixty files that import the loader.
Then it asks for a risk review.
Reviews keep missing issues in files near the middle of the pasted material.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Keep the diff and the list of importing paths in context.
Search for the loader's call patterns.
And read only matched ranges and direct callers.
Now the wrong turns.
Each one rearranges, shrinks, or splits the same flawed approach.
Wrong: paste the files after the question, so the recent material sits closest to the request.
Why?
That contradicts the placement guidance, which puts bulk first and the question last.
And it does nothing about density.
Wrong: split the sixty files into batches of ten, in separate sessions, and concatenate the reports.
Why?
It breaks the cross-file reasoning a blast-radius review needs.
No batch can see the others.
Wrong: paste only the ten most recently modified importers.
Why?
Recency is a proxy, not retrieval.
It misses importers that haven't changed lately.
The notes carry a sibling scenario worth knowing.
A prototype loads the twelve most recently modified files of a twenty-three-hundred-file repository into the system prompt, on every request.
Three things happen.
It answers questions about those twelve well.
It misses cross-file relationships.
And it gets worse on the loaded files as the conversation lengthens.
The right design keeps a lightweight index of paths and symbols.
It exposes search and ranged-read tools.
And it delegates wide exploration to a subagent.
That sibling scenario has three wrong turns too.
Wrong: load fifty recent files instead of twelve.
Why?
That scales the flaw.
Wrong: move the twelve files to the end of the context.
Why?
It misapplies a real principle.
Placement cannot help with the two thousand two hundred and eighty-eight files that are not there at all.
Wrong: concatenate the whole repository into one document.
Why?
It maximises cost.
And it will stop fitting after a year of growth anyway.
Takeaway.
Keep the list in the window, and fetch the pages when you need them.
The third concept is delegation.
And the part of delegation that actually matters.
The plain version.
You send an assistant to the archive.
If they come back saying "it all looked fine, mostly," you have to go yourself.
The trip was wasted.
If you tell them up front to bring back file numbers, page numbers, and what they didn't get to, their trip replaces yours.
In exam terms, a subagent runs with its own context.
The cost of forty searches and a dozen partial reads accrues in the subagent's window.
And it's discarded when the subagent finishes.
What returns is the conclusion.
In Claude Code, you can get this isolation in two ways.
From a subagent.
Or from a skill set to run in a forked context.
But the value of that isolation depends entirely on the return contract.
What does a good return sound like?
Something like this.
Authentication is enforced in the auth middleware file, lines forty-four to ninety-one.
Three handlers in the legacy handlers file register through a raw registration path that skips the middleware chain.
Here are their line numbers.
Here is the test that would have caught it.
And here is what was not examined.
That's a few hundred tokens, standing in for tens of thousands.
And it carries the identifiers the main session needs to act.
Question three.
Here's the scenario.
An exploration subagent, run as a forked-context skill, is asked why some legacy endpoints skip authentication.
It returns, "authentication looks mostly fine; a few legacy handlers might be worth a look."
The main session then re-reads the handler files itself.
That roughly doubles the cost of every investigation.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Specify the subagent's return contract.
Exact files and line ranges.
The bypass path.
The test that would catch it.
And what went unexamined.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: drop the subagent and explore in the main session.
Why?
It throws away the context isolation.
And it fills the main window with the very files the subagent existed to keep out.
Wrong: keep the design, but always re-read every file the subagent read.
Why?
That's the named anti-pattern of a coordinator re-reading what its subagents read.
Paying full cost twice, and calling it verification.
Wrong: run the subagent on a bigger model.
Why?
It produces a more fluent impression.
One that still lacks paths and line numbers.
The principle in the rulebook is short.
Hold on to this line.
Write the return contract before you delegate.
So when do you search in the main session, and when do you delegate?
Search directly when the question is narrow, and the hits will be few.
The map and a handful of ranged reads are cheap.
Delegate when the sweep will be wide, and the main session needs its room for the real work that follows.
Either way, what comes back should be identifiers, not impressions.
And a cross-reference.
The chapter on agent architecture warns against writing a delegation prompt as though the child shares your conversation.
A subagent starts with none of your context.
So the prompt must stand alone.
That's part four.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
Delegation buys you a discarded context, and the return contract is what makes the purchase worth it.
And this connects to what's next.
A conclusion returned from a subagent is a claim you eventually have to decide whether to trust, without redoing the work.
Coming up in part five: human review workflows and confidence calibration.
